doc.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998

title: Judy Garland and Mickey Rooney tour: leaving Denver for MGM
summary: Playing in a Denver hotel band, he was sent to replace the ill pianist on the MGM publicity tour with Judy and Mickey.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Didn’t you make your way to Hollywood with a chance encounter with Judy Garland?

Yeah. Yeah there was a troupe on the road. I was playing with this rinky-dink band in Colorado at a hotel which is now torn down mercifully, in Denver. And it sounds like a cheap film plot, but they came through, Judy and Mickey were starting to do the Andy Hardy series at MGM, it was the late ‘30s. And MGM sent them out on what we call a “trip to huckster everything.” And Mickey would do half of his father’s act. His father was a burlesque comic, Joe Ewell. And Mickey would do the clean part of his father’s act, and then Judy would sing a couple of songs and they’d show the film. It’s strange. And their second trip out was Denver, where their pianist became ill. I mean this could

never happen but it does. And a gentleman by the name of Frank Perquette was the tour manager for MGM so-called. And he called desperately to find somebody. He called the hotel. They lived in the hotel where I was playing with this so-called orchestra. And I think he called the hotel manager or something and asked if I could be sent down to help them out. And the hotel manager was wonderful, he said that I read music. And I thought that that was the most wonderful recommendation. And a day later here I am on the road for MGM.
And you gave a twelve hour notice to the rinky-dink orchestra.

Oh I doubt if I gave twelve hours. They were so in awe that I got this job, I think they harbored some respect for me. Three saxophones, two brass, a girl singer, the leader played violin, horrible, and his brother played drums. I can still visage the orchestra. And a bass player who constantly played out of tune.
Wow you’ve come a long way.
Not necessarily. We still have problems today.
